title: What If You Tried to Open a Plane Door Mid-Flight? ✈️
description:
Gus wakes up from a nap at 38,000 feet, mistakes the exit for the bathroom and pulls the handle with everything he has. Nothing happens, and this is the physics of why nothing can.

The numbers, for an airliner at cruise:
• 38,000 ft is 7.2 miles up; the air outside presses about a fifth as hard as at sea level (3.0 psi against 14.7 psi)
• The cabin is kept at the pressure of 8,000 ft or lower (10.9 psi), so the air inside pushes about 8 psi harder than the air outside
• A Boeing 737 entry door is 34 x 72 inches: 2,448 square inches
• 8 psi x 2,448 square inches is almost 20,000 pounds (about 9 tonnes), the weight of four average new cars
• The door is a plug: it is wider than its opening and has to move inward before it can swing out, against all of that
• A two-inch suction cup works the same way and can hold up to 46 pounds
(Assumptions: cruise at 38,000 ft, cabin at the 8,000 ft limit, standard atmosphere, a classic plug-type door. This is the cautious end: real jets hold a little more. Close to the ground the pressure difference shrinks to nothing, which is the only time a door can move. Please leave the handle alone anyway.)

Sources:
• 14 CFR 25.841, Pressurized cabins (cabin altitude of not more than 8,000 ft)
• U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976 / ICAO Standard Atmosphere
• Boeing, 737 Airplane Characteristics for Airport Planning (door size); 737 FCOM (pressure schedule)
• Patrick Smith, Ask the Pilot, "Open Door Policy"
• EPA Automotive Trends Report 2023 (average car weight)

Every number is computed in code and checked. Animation, narration and music are made with software and AI tools.
